t: Minimum Absolute Difference Between Two Values
o: Find the closest pair of indices holding a 1 and a 2 respectively (either order). Example 1: 1s at 0 and 5, 2 at 3; distances 3 and 2, so the answer is 2. Example 2 has no 2, so -1. With n <= 100 even brute force works, but a single left-to-right scan remembering the latest 1 and latest 2 solves it in O(n) and generalizes gracefully.
k: Track the most recent index of a 1 and of a 2 while scanning; whenever either appears and the other has been seen, update the best distance.

a.n: Approach 1: Single scan with last-seen indices
a.i: As we walk, the closest partner for the current 1 (or 2) is always the most recent occurrence of the other value, so keeping just the last two indices suffices.
s: At index i: if nums[i] == 1 and last2 >= 0, update ans with i - last2; if nums[i] == 2 and last1 >= 0, update ans with i - last1.
Return ans, or -1 if it stayed infinite.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant work per element.

a.n: Approach 2: Brute force over all pairs
a.i: Check every (i, j) with nums[i] = 1 and nums[j] = 2 and take the minimum absolute difference. Perfectly adequate at n <= 100 and the most literal reading of the problem.
s: Double loop over all index pairs.
If nums[i] == 1 and nums[j] == 2, update ans with abs(i - j).

w: Prefer the single-scan version; it is just as short and scales. Pitfall: updating last1/last2 must happen for every occurrence, not only when improving the answer. Edge cases: arrays with only 0s and 1s (no 2, return -1), adjacent 1 and 2 (answer 1). Follow-up: closest pair among three distinguished values, or closest pair by value difference instead of index.
